patient.chief_complaint: Painful vision loss in the left eye over 5 days
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Priya Nair is a 29-year-old right-handed South Asian woman who presents to the neurology inpatient service with a 5-day history of progressive painful blurring of vision in her left eye. She first noticed a mild ache behind her left eye four evenings ago, which she initially attributed to prolonged screen time. The following morning she observed that her vision in the left eye was blurry and that colors appeared dull and desaturated when she covered her right eye. The pain behind the left eye worsened with upward and lateral gaze movements. Over the subsequent three days her visual acuity in the left eye continued to decline to the point that she could not read text on her phone with the left eye alone. She also noticed that the pain woke her from sleep on one occasion. She presented to her primary care physician who noted a left afferent pupillary defect and referred her urgently to the emergency department. On further questioning, she recalls a distinct episode approximately 9 months ago in which she developed progressive numbness and a pins-and-needles sensation in her right leg from mid-thigh to the foot over the course of one week. The symptoms persisted for about 4 weeks before gradually improving. She was seen at an urgent care clinic where lumbar disc herniation was suspected; no imaging was performed. She now notes that she still has faint residual tingling in the right foot when she is fatigued or overheated, but the episode was otherwise felt to have resolved. She denies any prior episodes of vision loss, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, limb weakness, or bowel and bladder dysfunction. She denies recent fevers, rash, joint pain, oral ulcers, genital ulcers, Raynaud phenomenon, or recent viral illness. She has not traveled internationally and denies tick exposures.

results.title: Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria
results.authors: Thompson AJ, Banwell BL, Barkhof F, et al.
results.key_findings: Revised criteria allow CSF-specific oligoclonal bands to substitute for dissemination in time. Symptomatic and asymptomatic MRI lesions may both be used. DIS requires one or more T2 lesions in at least 2 of 4 CNS regions: periventricular, cortical/juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord.

results.title: Multiple sclerosis
results.authors: Reich DS, Lucchinetti CF, Calabresi PA.
results.key_findings: RRMS accounts for approximately 85% of MS cases at onset. High-efficacy disease-modifying therapies (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, alemtuzumab, cladribine) reduce relapse rates by 50-70% versus platform agents. Early treatment initiation is associated with better long-term outcomes.

results.title: MRI criteria for the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: MAGNIMS consensus guidelines
results.authors: Filippi M, Rocca MA, Ciccarelli O, et al.
results.key_findings: Lesions in periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord regions are the four MS-typical locations. Cortical lesions can be counted alongside juxtacortical lesions. Spinal cord lesions occur in approximately 80% of established MS patients.

output.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria require demonstration of dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT), or DIS plus CSF-specific oligoclonal bands. DIS is met by one or more T2 lesions in at least 2 of 4 characteristic CNS locations. DIT can be met by simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on a single MRI, a new T2 or enhancing lesion on follow-up MRI, or CSF-specific oligoclonal bands. Disease-modifying therapies for RRMS include platform agents (interferon-beta, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) and high-efficacy agents (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, alemtuzumab, cladribine); agent selection depends on disease activity, patient comorbidities, JCV serostatus, and reproductive planning.

interactions: Ferrous sulfate: no pharmacokinetic interaction expected with interferon-beta, glatiramer acetate, dimethyl fumarate, natalizumab, or ocrelizumab
contraindications: Natalizumab: contraindicated in patients with active or prior progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML); requires JC virus antibody index testing before initiation
Ocrelizumab / ofatumumab: do not administer live-attenuated vaccines during or after B-cell depleting therapy
Teriflunomide: contraindicated in women who are pregnant or who may become pregnant (teratogenic; accelerated elimination procedure required if conception is planned)
Fingolimod / siponimod / ozanimod: contraindicated with certain cardiac conduction abnormalities; first-dose cardiac monitoring required
warnings: Check JC virus antibody index before natalizumab initiation; elevated index (>0.9) substantially increases PML risk, particularly after 24 months of treatment
Monitor CBC with differential before and during dimethyl fumarate or teriflunomide therapy; withhold dimethyl fumarate if lymphocyte count <500 cells/microL for >6 months
Screen for hepatitis B and C and tuberculosis before initiating B-cell depleting or alemtuzumab therapy
Vaccination: administer all recommended live-attenuated vaccines at least 4 weeks, and inactivated vaccines at least 2 weeks, before initiating immunosuppressive DMTs
Fingolimod and siponimod require a baseline ECG and first-dose observation for bradyarrhythmia
output.formulary_status: Varies by agent; most require prior authorization
alternatives: Ocrelizumab (anti-CD20, high efficacy, IV infusion every 6 months)
Natalizumab (alpha-4 integrin, high efficacy, requires JCV monitoring)
Dimethyl fumarate (oral, moderate efficacy, monitor lymphocytes)
Glatiramer acetate (injectable, moderate efficacy, favorable safety profile)

useless_tools.rationale: EEG has no role in MS diagnosis; findings would be non-specific and do not contribute to DIS or DIT assessment.
CT is markedly inferior to MRI for identifying demyelinating plaques; ordering CT adds radiation and delays definitive imaging without diagnostic benefit.
No cardiac indication in this MS workup; echocardiography does not inform the demyelinating differential.
Cardiac monitoring is only indicated for first-dose fingolimod initiation — not part of the MS diagnostic workup.
FDG-PET is not indicated for MS diagnosis or relapse evaluation; it does not differentiate demyelination from mimics and carries substantial cost.

sequence_constraints.reason: Standard practice to confirm absence of mass effect or raised intracranial pressure on brain MRI before performing lumbar puncture

critical_actions: Obtain brain MRI with gadolinium (MS protocol) to establish DIS across periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord regions and DIT via simultaneous enhancing and non-enhancing lesions
Extend MRI to cervical and thoracic spinal cord with contrast to assess cord involvement and lesion morphology (short-segment peripherally located lesions favor MS over NMOSD)
Exclude NMOSD and MOGAD with AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG by cell-based assay before committing to an MS diagnosis and initiating DMT
Perform CSF analysis with paired serum to assess oligoclonal bands and IgG index (CSF-specific OCBs can substitute for DIT per McDonald 2017 when DIS is met)

Treat the acute optic neuritis relapse with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3-5 days) to accelerate visual recovery; plasma exchange reserved for steroid-refractory severe visual loss

Initiate a disease-modifying therapy after relapse stabilization and mimic exclusion; counsel the patient on platform versus high-efficacy agent choice, considering disease activity, lesion burden, JCV serostatus, and reproductive plans
Check JCV antibody index before considering natalizumab; administer all age-appropriate live-attenuated vaccines at least 4 weeks before starting immunosuppressive DMT
Supplement vitamin D to therapeutic levels and counsel on Uhthoff phenomenon, heat avoidance, and smoking cessation as modifiable lifestyle factors
contraindicated_actions: Do not attribute this presentation solely to isolated optic neuritis (CIS) without fully evaluating the prior remitted sensory episode and the MRI lesion burden — doing so would delay diagnosis of established RRMS
Do not start a DMT before excluding NMOSD and MOGAD; some MS DMTs (particularly natalizumab) may worsen NMOSD relapses
Do not diagnose MS without meeting McDonald 2017 criteria (DIS and DIT) and excluding better explanations
Do not initiate fingolimod without a baseline ECG and first-dose bradyarrhythmia monitoring
Do not prescribe teriflunomide to a woman of childbearing potential without confirmed effective contraception and discussion of accelerated elimination procedures
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance MS therapy — they do not prevent relapses or progression and carry significant long-term harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiating B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P-receptor modulators
key_reasoning_points: The prior episode of right leg numbness 9 months ago with objective residual signs (right Babinski sign, decreased vibration in right lower extremity) constitutes a second attack with objective clinical evidence — combined with the current optic neuritis, this patient has had at least two attacks with evidence of >=2 lesions, meeting McDonald 2017 criteria for RRMS on clinical grounds alone even before imaging and CSF

Brain MRI demonstrates DIS (periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial lesions) and DIT (simultaneous enhancing left optic nerve lesion and left periventricular lesion co-existing with multiple non-enhancing lesions on the same scan)

CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (5 bands unique to CSF) with elevated IgG index further support intrathecal inflammation and can substitute for DIT under McDonald 2017 in cases where DIT is otherwise unmet
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG must be sent by cell-based assay and must be negative before committing to MS — NMOSD and MOGAD are the most clinically important mimics in a young woman with optic neuritis

The left relative afferent pupillary defect, left eye red desaturation, and left optic disc swelling are all ipsilateral to the left optic nerve MRI enhancement — internal consistency of the laterality is essential for case validity

Short-segment (<2 vertebral segments) cord lesions involving <50% of the cord cross-section at C4-C5 and T5-T6 favor MS over NMOSD (which typically shows LETM >=3 segments with central cord involvement)
